title: The Fresh Scent of Cleaners Could Be Creating Indoor Air Pollution
summary: A room that smells like citrus or pine usually feels clean. But that scent may be a sign of chemistry happening in the air. Research led by Brandon Boor at Purdue University found that fragrance compounds from both conventional cleaners and botanical essential-oil products react rapidly indoors and generate nanoparticles — particles so small they can penetrate deep into the lungs. "We showed that indoor ozone reactions with fragrances from cleaning produce nanoparticles that carry a respiratory dose comparable to, or greater than, what you would experience from standing outside along a busy road," said Boor, an assistant professor of civil and construction engineering. "You're not seeing smoke, dust, or haze in the air. Instead, you think the air smells great so it must be clean." The chemistry isn't new. Atmospheric scientists have long known that plant compounds called terpenes — like pinene from pine trees — react with ozone to form tiny particles outdoors. But indoors, scented cleaners release terpenes such as pinene, limonene (lemon), thymol (thyme), and linalool (lavender) at concentrations tens or even hundreds of times higher than in a forest. To test what happens in real life, Boor's team used a model home on Purdue's campus with a working kitchen, wood floors, and a bathroom. They cleaned with scented sprays, wipes, and liquid products. Routine tasks like mopping and wiping countertops generated billions or trillions of particles, most measuring only 1–30 nanometers across. That's below the detection range of most at-home air quality monitors, so people may have no idea particle levels have spiked. The researchers presented their findings at the American Chemical Society's fall meeting. The good news: exposure can be reduced by choosing unscented products, improving ventilation with exhaust fans or open windows, and avoiding ozone-generating devices while cleaning with scented products. Cleaning still removes viruses and bacteria — but the smell of "clean" may come with an invisible cost.
why_it_matters: Most people spend the vast majority of their lives indoors, yet indoor air is far less regulated and far less monitored than outdoor air, so a finding that everyday cleaning can create lung-penetrating particles at road-side levels raises hard questions about product labelling, building ventilation standards and who gets to know what they are breathing.

background_read: Ozone (a gas made of three oxygen atoms) is a protective shield high in the atmosphere, but at ground level it is a pollutant: it forms when sunlight hits traffic and industrial fumes, and it can drift indoors through open windows and ventilation systems.

Chemists have studied the ozone-terpene reaction outdoors for decades — pine forests release pinene, and that chemistry is one reason forests and cities both produce tiny suspended particles called aerosols.

Terpenes are the chemicals behind the smell of pine, lemon, lavender and thyme, and they are added to cleaning products to make them smell fresh, so a single spray can push indoor terpene levels far above anything found in nature.

Particles below about 100 nanometres are called ultrafine. They are measured in nanometres (billionths of a metre), which is why ordinary home air-quality monitors, which mainly track the larger PM2.5 particles, tend to miss them completely.

Purdue University (a large engineering-focused research university in Indiana, USA) built the model home so the team could clean and measure in a realistic kitchen and bathroom, and the results were presented at a meeting of the American Chemical Society (the world's largest professional society for chemists), meaning they have been shared with other scientists but may not yet have gone through full peer review.

perspectives.description: Cleaning still does its main job of removing germs, and the fix is cheap and immediate: choose unscented products and open a window. Making people aware that a fresh smell is not the same as clean air is itself a useful public health message.

Ingredient lists often hide fragrance blends behind a single word, protected as trade secrets, so shoppers cannot avoid what they cannot see. Critics argue that marketing freshness as a health signal misleads people, and that regulators have been slow to treat indoor air chemistry as a real exposure risk.

This is an old story with a new setting. Cooking, candles, printers and gas stoves have long been known to generate indoor particles; the modern twist is that energy-efficient buildings are sealed tighter, letting pollutants build up. The terpene-ozone reaction was documented outdoors decades ago — what changed is where it now happens.

The next step is measurement: affordable sensors that can see ultrafine particles, plus building codes that require real ventilation rather than just air conditioning. If the findings hold up in peer review and in ordinary homes, labels and product design may have to change too.
